{"url": "https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=all%3Aintrinsic+motivation+frameworks+for+active+learning+and+epistemic+curiosity+in+scientific+discovery+agents&max_results=4", "scope": "paper abstracts; preprints, peer-review status not verified", "excerpt": "title: Curiosity-Critic: Cumulative Prediction Error Improvement as a Tractable Intrinsic Reward for World Model Training
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18701v3
published: 2026-04-20T18:01:15Z
summary: Local prediction-error-based curiosity rewards focus on the current transition without considering the world model's cumulative prediction error across all visited transitions. We introduce Curiosity-Critic, which grounds its intrinsic reward in the improvement of this cumulative objective, and show that it admits a tractable per-step surrogate: the difference between the current prediction error and the asymptotic error baseline of the current state transition. We estimate this error baseline online with a learned critic co-trained alongside the world model; since the critic only has to learn how hard a transition is to predict, its estimate of the irreducible noise floor converges well before the world model saturates, redirecting exploration toward learnable transitions. The reward is higher for learnable transitions and collapses toward zero for stochastic ones, thereby separating epistemic (reducible) from aleatoric (irreducible) prediction error online. Prior prediction-error curiosity formulations, from Schmidhuber (1991) to learned-feature-space variants, emerge as special cases corresponding to specific approximations of this error baseline. Experiments on a stochastic grid world show that Curiosity-Critic outperforms prediction-error, visitation-count, and Random Network Distillation methods in training speed and final world model accuracy.

title: Computational Theories of Curiosity-Driven Learning
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/1802.10546v2
published: 2018-02-28T17:28:25Z
summary: What are the functions of curiosity? What are the mechanisms of curiosity-driven learning? We approach these questions about the living using concepts and tools from machine learning and developmental robotics. We argue that curiosity-driven learning enables organisms to make discoveries to solve complex problems with rare or deceptive rewards. By fostering exploration and discovery of a diversity of behavioural skills, and ignoring these rewards, curiosity can be efficient to bootstrap learning when there is no information, or deceptive information, about local improvement towards these problems. We also explain the key role of curiosity for efficient learning of world models. We review both normative and heuristic computational frameworks used to understand the mechanisms of curiosity in humans, conceptualizing the child as a sense-making organism. These frameworks enable us to discuss the bi-directional causal links between curiosity and learning, and to provide new hypotheses about the fundamental role of curiosity in self-organizing developmental structures through curriculum learning. We present various developmental robotics experiments that study these mechanisms in action, both supporting these hypotheses to understand better curiosity in humans and opening new research avenues in machine learning and artificial intelligence. Finally, we discuss challenges for the design of experimental paradigms for studying curiosity in psychology and cognitive neuroscience.
  Keywords: Curiosity, intrinsic motivation, lifelong learning, predictions, world model, rewards, free-energy principle, learning progress, machine learning, AI, developmental robotics, development, curriculum learning, self-organization.

title: Large-Scale Study of Curiosity-Driven Learning
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/1808.04355v1
published: 2018-08-13T17:58:01Z
summary: Reinforcement learning algorithms rely on carefully engineering environment rewards that are extrinsic to the agent. However, annotating each environment with hand-designed, dense rewards is not scalable, motivating the need for developing reward functions that are intrinsic to the agent. Curiosity is a type of intrinsic reward function which uses prediction error as reward signal. In this paper: (a) We perform the first large-scale study of purely curiosity-driven learning, i.e. without any extrinsic rewards, across 54 standard benchmark environments, including the Atari game suite. Our results show surprisingly good performance, and a high degree of alignment between the intrinsic curiosity objective and the hand-designed extrinsic rewards of many game environments. (b) We investigate the effect of using different feature spaces for computing prediction error and show that random features are sufficient for many popular RL game benchmarks, but learned features appear to generalize better (e.g. to novel game levels in Super Mario Bros.). (c) We demonstrate limitations of the prediction-based rewards in stochastic setups. Game-play videos and code are at https://pathak22.github.io/large-scale-curiosity/

title: Bootstrapping Intrinsically Motivated Learning with Human Demonstrations
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/1112.1937v1
published: 2011-12-08T20:27:31Z
summary: This paper studies the coupling of internally guided learning and social interaction, and more specifically the improvement owing to demonstrations of the learning by intrinsic motivation. We present Socially Guided Intrinsic Motivation by Demonstration (SGIM-D), an algorithm for learning in continuous, unbounded and non-preset environments. After introducing social learning and intrinsic motivation, we describe the design of our algorithm, before showing through a fishing experiment that SGIM-D efficiently combines the advantages of social learning and intrinsic motivation to gain a wide repertoire while being specialised in specific subspaces.", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "d24a96501f6f488142cc1dce97c05145d3610a22bbcfb3f1a141269b13f152ef", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unassigned_inquiry", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["arxiv:2604.18701v3", "arxiv:1802.10546v2", "arxiv:1808.04355v1", "arxiv:1112.1937v1"], "source_candidates": [], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

AI-assisted peer review: efficiency for reviewers, burden for authors—a narrative review
A

Article metrics

Abstract
Artificial intelligence (AI) in scholarly peer review has the potential to simplify the work of editors and reviewers through faster triage, automated reporting completeness checks, and scalable synthesis of reviewer comments. However, it also presents practical, ethical, and technical limitations that may place implementation burdens on authors. I examine bias arising from training data and model architecture, confidentiality risks from commercial AI deployment, accountability gaps when human judgment is displaced, and the growing threat of hallucinated citations to scientific integrity. I further analyze how poorly governed AI integration shifts remediation and formatting burdens onto authors—particularly those from under-resourced or non-Western institutions. I propose hybrid human–AI workflows, mandatory disclosure standards, and equity-conscious implementation frameworks to address these harms. Responsible AI integration in peer review requires transparency, human accountability, and deliberate protection of the diversity of voices represented in scientific literature. These considerations also extend beyond individual actors to recursive feedback loops in which AI-assisted manuscripts are evaluated by AI-assisted review systems, reinforcing the need for human contextual stewardship.
1 Introduction
The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed various aspects of scientific research, including academic publishing and peer review. Large language models and other AI tools have proven in recent years to be capable of automating many tasks that have historically been performed by human editors and reviewers. Automated language and grammar checks, plagiarism detection, format compliance, and even preliminary evaluation of research significance are some of these applications (
Doskaliuk et al., 2025
).
Early implementations indicate that AI can effectively detect common omissions, highlight internal inconsistencies, and produce structured summaries that assist editors and reviewers, potentially increasing

7.6 Limitations and caveats
Nevertheless, these efficiency gains must be carefully balanced against substantive risks. Cognitive offloading—the tendency to delegate analytical effort to AI systems—can erode the depth and independence of human judgment over time, with reviewers placing excessive trust in algorithmically generated assessments even when errors are present (
Gerlich, 2025
). Additionally, the systemic biases inherent to AI models trained predominantly on English-language and Western-institution data risk propagating methodological and geographic prejudices into reviewer feedback (
Hosseini and Horbach, 2023
). These considerations collectively underscore the irreplaceable role of human judgment and ethical accountability as foundational imperatives within any AI-augmented peer review paradigm (
Walshe et al., 2025
).
8 How AI in peer review complicates implementation for authors
While AI-assisted peer review promises efficiency gains for editors and reviewers, it can simultaneously create significant implementation burdens for authors—particularly those from under-resourced or non-Western institutions. Beyond administrative and formatting demands, authors face a deeper and more consequential set of complications rooted in confidentiality risks, algorithmic bias, intellectual property vulnerability, and systemic epistemic inequity, each of which is examined below.
8.1 Confidentiality and intellectual property risks
A fundamental concern pertains to manuscript confidentiality. When peer reviewers, editors, or automated submission systems upload unpublished

9 Conclusion
AI in peer review offers real efficiency gains for editors and reviewers, but these benefits can impose downstream costs on authors through false positives, algorithmic bias, opaque feedback, and undisclosed AI use. Published evidence of fabricated citations, prompt-sensitive bias, and variable agreement with human reviewers demonstrates that efficiency without accountability can threaten scientific integrity (
Walters and Wilder, 2023
;
Suleiman et al., 2024
;
Liang et al., 2024a
;
Teixeira, 2025
).
Responsible integration demands transparency about AI use, human accountability for all editorial decisions, and equity-conscious design that prevents burden transferring onto authors least equipped to absorb it. Journals should mandate AI disclosure, conduct regular bias audits, and establish author feedback mechanisms to monitor false-positive burdens.
Without these safeguards, AI-assisted peer review risks narrowing the diversity of voices, methods, and knowledge systems that science depends upon. AI can strengthen peer review—but only when governed with the same rigor science demands of the research it evaluates. Governance must also address the recursive author–AI–reviewer feedback loop at the system level, preserving human contextual stewardship as a deliberate safeguard against self-reinforcing errors and epistemic narrowing (
Biele and Kowalski, 2026
).
